note: Synthetic incident narratives for training only. All names are fictional (example.test). Each step is one attacker action.

steps.text: The attacker reads public blog posts, job adverts and conference slides of Example Corp to learn which LLM vendor and vector database the support copilot uses.
The attacker registers a look-alike domain and sets up a web page to host a poisoned document, and buys cloud credits to run their own tooling.
The attacker sends a support email that contains hidden instructions; the copilot ingests it when it summarises the shared inbox.
The attacker queries the public chat endpoint of the copilot with many test prompts through the product API to see how it behaves.
The hidden instructions make the copilot run a tool call to the ticket-search function with attacker-chosen arguments.
The injected text is written into the copilot's long-term memory, so it stays active in every future session.
The copilot gathers customer records from the CRM tool that match the attacker's request.
The copilot renders a markdown image whose URL carries the stolen records out to a server the attacker controls.

incidents.title: Look-alike model on a public hub

steps.text: The attacker trains a backdoored classifier and uploads it to a public model hub under a name similar to a popular model, preparing the malicious artifact in advance.
A developer downloads the look-alike model into the CI pipeline: a supply chain compromise through a trusted-looking source.
Loading the unsafe pickle file executes the embedded code (a harmless canary in this exercise) on the build agent.
The embedded code steals the cloud access keys and tokens stored in environment variables of the build agent.
The attacker lists the storage buckets, registry entries and service accounts that the stolen keys can reach.
Using an over-permissive role, the attacker escalates to admin rights on the ML platform.
The attacker renames files, splits the payload and obfuscates it so the model scanner does not detect it.
The poisoned model is deployed and starts approving fraudulent loans, causing financial loss and harm to customers.

incidents.title: Fraud detector evasion and model theft

steps.text: Researchers read the vendor's published papers and model cards to identify the architecture of the fraud-detection model.
They obtain a paid API key and send thousands of queries to the scoring endpoint to get access to the model's outputs.
They train a proxy model on the collected responses and craft adversarial examples offline against that proxy.
They apply the crafted perturbations so that fraudulent transactions look legitimate and evade the detector.
They gather training datasets and prompt logs from an exposed data lake.
They copy the model weights from an unprotected storage bucket to a server they own, an exfiltration of the model.
Fraudulent transactions pass unnoticed and the bank suffers financial loss and reputational damage.

incidents.title: Denial of wallet through a leaked key

steps.text: The attacker scans public code repositories and search engines for information about which company runs an LLM gateway.
The attacker uses a stolen API key to sign in to the gateway as a valid account.
The attacker finds an API key for the gateway in a configuration file and extracts the credentials from it.
The attacker asks the model which tools, plugins and data sources it has access to, discovering its capabilities.
The attacker sends long prompts in a loop, causing a flood of expensive requests that exhaust the monthly budget and make the service unavailable.
